<Rep. Jamie Raskin>: I oppose H.R. 2243, the LEOSA Reform Act.
In 2004, Congress passed the Law Enforcement Officer Safety Act (LEOSA), a law that allows both off-duty and retired law enforcement officers to carry concealed firearms irrespective of state law. LEOSA preempted states' judgments about what was best for their communities and their residents, forcing all states to allow off-duty and retired law enforcement to carry concealed firearms under the terms set by Congress.
As Congress debated LEOSA more than 20 years ago, Members of this Committee on both sides of the aisle expressed concerns about how the bill violated the principles of federalism and undermined states' rights. The Republican Chairman of the Judiciary Committee at the time, Congressman Sensenbrenner, opposed LEOSA for this reason.\1\ Several police groups also opposed this legislation and expressed concerns about how it would affect officer safety, how it could create more confusion in responding to active shooters, how it might expose their agencies to more liability when officers carried under LEOSA, and the insufficiency of requirements for retired officers.
\1\Law Enforcement Officers Safety Act of 2003, H. Rept. 108-560, 108th Cong. (2004).
Despite these concerns, LEOSA became law--though it did include some important limitations and imposed commonsense training requirements, which have been in place for more than 20 years.
H.R. 2243, the LEOSA Reform Act, would end what little right states have to limit when and where individuals may carry concealed firearms under LEOSA. It would force states to allow retired and current officers to carry concealed firearms onto private property open to the public, including restaurants, bars, parks, and playgrounds. It would also force states to allow off-duty and retired officers to carry concealed firearms on buses, trains, and subways. And it would even force states to allow for the concealed carry of firearms in Gun-Free School Zones. H.R. 2243 also allows off-duty and retired law enforcement officers to completely disregard state laws prohibiting high-capacity magazines.
This legislation not only supersedes the judgment of the states, but it also threatens the safety and security of federal agencies by forcing them to allow concealed carry under LEOSA in many federal buildings. Forcing federal offices and buildings to allow concealed carry in these places is a completely unnecessary risk.
Another troubling aspect of this legislation is that it weakens training standards. Under current law, a person carrying a firearm under LEOSA must meet state training requirements every year, but H.R. 2243 would allow individuals to concealed carry with training certification as sparingly as every three years. This is troubling given that the bill extends nationwide concealed carry to retired officers who are no longer receiving the training that accompanies their employment.
All of these expansions are profoundly risky given the large number of people this new law would apply to: we know there are more than 700,000 active law enforcement officers nationwide.\2\ And while we don't know the exact number of retired officers in the United States, we know this number has increased significantly in recent years as many police departments across the country have faced sharp increases in retirement rates. One study found that there are four retired officers and four resigned officers for every 100 active officers each year.\3\ Therefore, the universe of people this bill would apply to is substantial.
\2\Law Enforcement Employees Reported by the United States (see table, ``Law Enforcement Employees Breakout''), FBI Crime Data Explorer, https://cde.ucr.cjis.gov/LATEST/webapp/#/pages/le/pe (last visited Apr. 22, 2025); Law Enforcement Facts: Key Data About the Profession, National Law Enforcement Memorial Fund, https://nleomf.org/ memorial/facts-figures/law-enforcement-facts/ (last visited Apr. 18, 2025).
\3\PERF Special Report, Police Executive Research Forum (Jun. 11, 2021) https://www. policeforum.org/workforcesurveyjune2021.
Of course, our colleagues wish it were the case that a ``good guy'' with a gun is the answer to a ``bad guy'' with a gun, but the research does not bear this out. Studies show that individuals successfully defend themselves with a gun in less than 1% of crimes involving personal contact.\4\ Gun accidents and unnecessary escalation are pervasive threats.
\4\Gaby Blanco & Rafael Medina, RELEASE: New CAP Analysis Debunks Myths About Defensive Gun Use, Center for American Progress (Feb. 12, 2024), https://www. americanprogress.org/press/release-do-guns-make-us-safer-debunking-myths-about-defensive-gun-use/.
We have dozens of legislative proposals that we know would make our communities safer, while still respecting states' rights. This bill is not one of them.
I urge all my colleagues to oppose this legislation.
Jamie Raskin,
Ranking Member.
